chapter: Joe Liggins and back to Kid Ory
title: New Orleans musicians and classical music
summary: Joe admits he rarely listened to classical music, though his father owned records, and the French Opera never being rebuilt; he praises trumpeter P.G. Laurie.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Well, I'm saying that to say this. In your estimation... Well, at least to me, talking about this very thing with Tudie... This is why I brought this whole thing up. Jazz musicians, the New Orleans bunch, at least to me, they talk about... Like you were saying about the Bix Beiderbecke records, they heard this, they heard that. Very few of them ever say they heard any Classical music. Would you say that New Orleans musicians were basically not interested in Classical music?
When I was a kid, my Dad used to have a lot of Classical records. We had a phonograph. But I...

But I mean, the average New Orleans musician will know Louis' record of so-and-so, he'll know Jack Teagarden's record of so-and-so, Bix Beiderbecke's record, or even Dizzy Gillespie's record, no matter what. But if you ask him about Classical things... You never said you listened to Classical music at all.

I never did. There was a few Classical records that I had. I remember when I went out as a kid, I had to play the pretty thing on that tune...[SINGS REFRAIN] -- Rose of Washington Square, that a symphony had made. And another tune called Mickey that was from one of the operas or something. I remember a couple of those

records I used to listen to. Another thing, we had records of some marches that Souza made that we used to listen to. Moreso than the Dixieland records. Like I told you, another thing, the first things I remember about Dixieland was the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, Livery Stable Blues and those old tunes, and then here comes old Ben Pollack -- stuff like that.

You said before... This is going way back, to the first tape, but I still want to talk about this for a little bit longer. You said before that the French Opera in New Orleans was a place where they played Classics, operettas, operas and all that. After the French Opera burned down, was there any other place that people could go?

No. That was one of the sad things. My Dad used to talk about it all the time. That ended the opera. They never did rebuild. And they always talked about it. Papa used to say, 'Well, they're going to build the French Opera; I'll be glad when I'll be able to go to shows.'

Well, that's the whole point I was getting at. I thought maybe it might have something to do with when the French Opera burned down there was no Classical music available in the city much to listen to in the flesh.

Because very few of the older New Orleans musicians know anything about Classical music whatsoever. They know more about Motown music or any crazy...Country-and-Western Music. But Classical music, very few of them know anything about it. They couldn't recognize Mozart from Beethoven. And I wonder if there was anywhere else in New Orleans that you could hear Classical music after the French Opera burned down. But you say no.

No. Well, a lot of it ended. But the thing about it which was a good thing, that Opera left... A lot of those good musicians stayed in New Orleans and taught, you see. One of the great Black musicians you don't hear about, that could play Classics, was named P.G. Laurie -- he had a band on the Ringling Brothers Circus. He wasn't from New Orleans. But he was a good trumpet player. Riddell(?) Clark, who is one of your great trumpet virtuosos, who lives in Long Beach, says P.G. Laurie(?) was one of your great trumpet players. It's a pity he wasn't White. In Ringling Brothers Circus he couldn't play in the Big Top.
We'd better move on a bit more.
